question: A 45-year-old woman presents with 18 months of slowly progressive painless axial proptosis of the right eye. Visual acuity is 6/9, colour vision is slightly reduced, and there is no pain on eye movement. CT orbit shows a well-defined, round, intraconal lesion with progressive enhancement on contrast injection ('patchy then homogeneous' pattern). Which is the MOST likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orbital lymphoma typically moulds around orbital structures ('cast sign' or 'salmon patch' under the conjunctiva in MALT lymphoma), is often extraconal, and does not show the progressive patchy-to-homogeneous enhancement on dynamic CT that characterises cavernous haemangioma. Lymphoma tends to diffusely infiltrate rather than form a discrete round intraconal mass.

Optic nerve glioma arises from the optic nerve itself, producing a fusiform enlargement of the nerve ('kinking' of the optic nerve on CT/MRI). It presents with vision loss and proptosis but the mass is centred on the nerve, not a separate intraconal lesion beside it. It is most common in children with neurofibromatosis type 1.

Correct. Cavernous haemangioma (now reclassified as venous malformation) is the commonest benign intraconal orbital tumour in adults. Classic features: middle-aged woman, slowly progressive painless axial proptosis, well-defined round/oval mass on CT, and the pathognomonic progressive (patchy → homogeneous) contrast enhancement due to slow filling of endothelium-lined vascular lakes. Treatment is surgical excision (lateral orbitotomy) if vision is compromised.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest primary orbital MALIGNANCY in children (not adults), presenting with RAPID onset proptosis over days to weeks — very unlike the 18-month history here. In an adult with a well-defined intraconal mass and progressive enhancement, rhabdomyosarcoma is extremely unlikely.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key clues: adult, female, SLOW (months), AXIAL (intraconal), WELL-DEFINED, PROGRESSIVE enhancement = cavernous haemangioma. Rhabdomyosarcoma = child, rapid. Lymphoma = moulds, extraconal. Glioma = centred on nerve. Memorise this pattern for finals.

Correct. Cavernous haemangioma: middle-aged woman, slow painless proptosis, well-defined intraconal mass, progressive CT enhancement = the classic teaching case in orbital tumours (Khurana Chapter 21).
